questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 3 · Minimum subscribers
questions.stem: Under section 3(1) of the Companies Act 2013, the minimum number of persons who must subscribe their names to the memorandum for the formation of a public company is:

readLink.label: Read: Formation of a company — ss. 3 and 3A →

options.text: One
options.explanation: One person forms a One Person Company under s. 3(1)(c), which is a private company — never a public company.

options.text: Two
options.explanation: Two is the private-company minimum under s. 3(1)(b). The stem asks about a public company.

options.text: Seven
options.explanation: Section 3(1)(a) requires seven or more persons for a public company; they need not all be natural persons.

options.text: Fifty
options.explanation: Fifty is the ceiling on the number of members of a private company under s. 2(68); it is not a formation minimum for any company.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 3(2) · Classes by liability
questions.stem: Section 3(2) permits a company formed under section 3(1) to be of certain kinds. Which of the following is NOT a kind of company recognised by section 3(2)?

readLink.label: Read: Formation of a company — ss. 3 and 3A →

options.text: A company limited by shares
options.explanation: Expressly recognised by s. 3(2)(a).

options.text: A company limited by the number of its members
options.explanation: There is no such kind. Section 3(2) classifies companies by the extent of members' LIABILITY — shares, guarantee or unlimited. The number of members is a s. 3(1) question, not a s. 3(2) one; the two tests are being confused.

options.text: A company limited by guarantee
options.explanation: Expressly recognised by s. 3(2)(b), with or without share capital.

options.text: An unlimited company
options.explanation: Expressly recognised by s. 3(2)(c).

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 3(1)(c) Explanation · OPC nominee
questions.stem: Regarding the nominee whose name an OPC's memorandum must indicate, which statement is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Formation of a company — ss. 3 and 3A →

options.text: The nominee must give his prior written consent, and he becomes the member on the subscriber's death or incapacity to contract
options.explanation: That is exactly the Explanation to s. 3(1): prior written consent, filed with the Registrar, and the nominee steps in on death or incapacity to contract.

options.text: The nominee is a member of the OPC from the date of incorporation, jointly with the subscriber
options.explanation: An OPC has only one member. The nominee holds nothing but a right to step in later; treating him as a present member turns the OPC into a two-member company.

options.text: Once given, the nomination is irrevocable and the nominee cannot withdraw his consent
options.explanation: The nominee may withdraw his consent and the member may change the nominee at any time; a fresh nomination and intimation to the Registrar follow.

options.text: The nominee becomes the member only on the subscriber's death, and not on his incapacity to contract
options.explanation: The Explanation names two triggers — death AND incapacity to contract. Dropping the second is the standard misreading.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 3A · Nature of the liability
questions.stem: Where the membership of a company falls below the statutory minimum and it carries on business for more than six months, section 3A makes liable:

readLink.label: Read: Formation of a company — ss. 3 and 3A →

options.text: Every member of the company, jointly and severally, for all debts of the company whenever contracted
options.explanation: Two errors: liability is SEVERAL, not joint and several, and it covers only debts contracted after the six months while the company is short-handed.

options.text: Every person who is a member during the time the company so carries on business after those six months and who is cognisant of the fact, severally, for the debts contracted during that time
options.explanation: That is s. 3A word for word in substance — cognisance, several liability, and only the debts contracted during the period of continued short-handed trading.

options.text: The directors and key managerial personnel of the company, severally
options.explanation: Section 3A reaches MEMBERS, not officers. Directors face consequences elsewhere in the Act, not under this section.

options.text: Every member, whether or not he knows of the reduction, for debts contracted from the date the number fell
options.explanation: Both limbs are wrong: only members COGNISANT of the fact are caught, and the clock starts only when the six months expire.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 3A · Six-month clock
questions.stem: The membership of Deccan Alloys Limited, a public company, falls to five on 12 June 2026 and the company continues to trade. The six-month period allowed by section 3A expires on:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 3A — six months of continued trading

readLink.label: Read: Formation of a company — ss. 3 and 3A →

options.text: 12 September 2026
options.explanation: That is three months. Section 3A allows six months of continued trading, not three.

options.text: 9 December 2026
options.explanation: That is 180 days counted day by day. Section 3A speaks of six MONTHS, so the calendar-month count from 12 June gives 12 December.

options.text: 12 December 2026
options.explanation: Six calendar months from 12 June 2026. Debts contracted after this date, while the company is still short of seven members, attract several liability on cognisant members.

options.text: 12 June 2027
options.explanation: That is twelve months. No twelve-month grace exists under s. 3A.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 3 · Restoring the minimum
questions.stem: Konkan Marine Limited, a public company, had eleven members. Six of them transfer their entire holdings to the remaining members, so that the company now has five members. To restore the statutory minimum for a public company, the minimum number of additional members that must be brought on the register is:

readLink.label: Read: Formation of a company — ss. 3 and 3A →

options.text: One
options.explanation: One would take the roll to six, still one short of the seven required by s. 3(1)(a).

options.text: Six
options.explanation: Six restores the original eleven, but the statutory floor is seven, not the number the company happened to have before.

options.text: Two
options.explanation: Seven less the present five gives two. Bring them in within six months of the fall and s. 3A never engages.

options.text: Nil — once incorporated, a public company may function with any number of members
options.explanation: Incorporation does not freeze the position: s. 3A attaches several liability to cognisant members if short-handed trading continues beyond six months.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 2(69) · Who is a promoter
questions.stem: Which of the following persons is NOT a promoter within section 2(69) of the Companies Act 2013?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 2(69) and its proviso

readLink.label: Read: Promoters and pre-incorporation contracts →

options.text: A person identified by the company as a promoter in the annual return referred to in section 92
options.explanation: Limb (a) of s. 2(69) covers a person named as a promoter in a prospectus OR identified as such in the annual return.

options.text: A person who has control over the affairs of the company indirectly, otherwise than as a director
options.explanation: Limb (b) catches control exercised directly or indirectly, as shareholder, director or otherwise.

options.text: A person in accordance with whose instructions the Board is accustomed to act
options.explanation: Limb (c) catches exactly this, subject only to the professional-capacity proviso.

options.text: A chartered accountant in practice on whose professional advice as to the valuation of a business the Board acts
options.explanation: The proviso to s. 2(69) excludes a person acting MERELY in a professional capacity. Advising on a valuation is professional work; it becomes promotion only if he also does promoter acts, such as nominating the first directors or negotiating the acquisition.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Promoter · Fiduciary position
questions.stem: A promoter sells his own property to the company he is forming at a profit, without disclosing his interest to an independent Board or to the members. The company's remedies are:
questions.sourceRef: ICAI SM P2 Ch 2 — fiduciary position of a promoter

readLink.label: Read: Promoters and pre-incorporation contracts →

options.text: None — a promoter is neither an agent nor a trustee of the company, so he owes it no duty
options.explanation: He is indeed neither agent nor trustee, but he stands in a FIDUCIARY relation to the company; the absence of agency does not mean the absence of duty.

options.text: It may rescind the contract, or retain the property and recover the undisclosed profit, or sue for damages for breach of fiduciary duty
options.explanation: These are the three remedies for an undisclosed promoter's profit; the company elects between them.

options.text: It may only ratify the sale, since the property has already passed
options.explanation: Ratification is the company's choice, not its only option; the very point of the fiduciary rule is that the company may undo the transaction or strip the profit.

options.text: It must apply to the Tribunal, which alone can set aside a promoter's contract
options.explanation: No Tribunal sanction is needed. This confuses the promoter's fiduciary liability with the NCLT's powers under s. 7(7) over a fraudulently obtained incorporation.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Pre-incorporation contracts
questions.stem: Promoters of a company to be incorporated enter into a contract for the supply of machinery in the company's proposed name. After incorporation the Board passes a resolution ratifying the contract. The correct position is:
questions.sourceRef: ICAI SM P2 Ch 2 — pre-incorporation (preliminary) contracts

readLink.label: Read: Promoters and pre-incorporation contracts →

options.text: The Board's ratification makes the contract binding on the company from the date it was made
options.explanation: Ratification relates back to the date of the act and therefore requires a principal in existence THEN. The company was not, so nothing relates back.

options.text: The contract binds the company automatically on incorporation, without any resolution
options.explanation: Incorporation does not sweep up contracts made before it; the company acquires capacity only from the date in the certificate under s. 9.

options.text: The contract is void and the supplier has no remedy against anyone
options.explanation: The supplier is not remediless — the promoters are personally liable, and the contract may in a proper case be adopted under the Specific Relief Act.

options.text: The company cannot ratify the contract; the promoters remain personally liable unless the company enters into a fresh contract on the same terms
options.explanation: A company cannot ratify a pre-incorporation contract because it did not exist when the contract was made. Novation after incorporation is the cure.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Specific Relief Act ss. 15(h) / 19(e)
questions.stem: Under sections 15(h) and 19(e) of the Specific Relief Act 1963, a pre-incorporation contract may be specifically enforced by or against the company where:
questions.sourceRef: Specific Relief Act 1963, ss. 15(h) and 19(e), as stated in ICAI SM P2 Ch 2

readLink.label: Read: Promoters and pre-incorporation contracts →

options.text: The company has been registered within six months of the contract, irrespective of its objects
options.explanation: No such time condition exists. The conditions are about the terms of incorporation and communicated acceptance, not the speed of registration.

options.text: The contract is warranted by the terms of the incorporation and the company has accepted it and communicated the acceptance to the other party
options.explanation: Both conditions are cumulative: the contract must be warranted by the terms of the incorporation, and acceptance must be communicated to the other party.

options.text: The promoters have been reimbursed their preliminary expenses by the company
options.explanation: Reimbursement of preliminary expenses is unrelated; a promoter has no legal right to it in the first place.

options.text: The Central Government approves the adoption of the contract
options.explanation: No governmental approval is involved. This confuses the Specific Relief Act route with the approvals needed under ss. 13 and 14.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 7(1)(b) · Declaration on registration
questions.stem: The declaration filed under section 7(1)(b) that all requirements of the Act and the rules in respect of registration have been complied with must be made by:

readLink.label: Read: The incorporation process — s. 7 →

options.text: Every subscriber to the memorandum
options.explanation: Subscribers make the declaration under s. 7(1)(c) about convictions and the correctness of the documents — a different declaration with different content.

options.text: The Registrar of Companies before whom the documents are filed
options.explanation: The Registrar receives the declaration; he does not make it.

options.text: Any practising professional, whether or not engaged in the formation of the company
options.explanation: The section requires the professional to be one who is ENGAGED IN THE FORMATION of the company; an unconnected professional will not do.

options.text: An advocate, chartered accountant, cost accountant or company secretary in practice engaged in the formation of the company, AND a person named in the articles as a director, manager or secretary
options.explanation: Section 7(1)(b) requires both limbs — the practising professional engaged in the formation, and a first officer named in the articles.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 7(1)(c) · Subscriber and director declaration
questions.stem: The declaration required from each subscriber and each person named as a first director under section 7(1)(c) covers, among other things, that he has not been found guilty of any fraud, misfeasance or breach of duty to any company during the preceding:

readLink.label: Read: The incorporation process — s. 7 →

options.text: Three years
options.explanation: Three years is the trade-mark window in s. 16(1)(b), not the look-back in the s. 7(1)(c) declaration.

options.text: Five years
options.explanation: Section 7(1)(c) uses a five-year look-back for fraud, misfeasance or breach of duty, alongside the declaration that all documents filed contain correct and complete information.

options.text: Ten years
options.explanation: No ten-year period appears anywhere in s. 7.

options.text: One year
options.explanation: One year is far short of the statutory look-back; the conviction limb of the same declaration carries no time limit at all.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 7(7) · NCLT powers
questions.stem: Where a company has been got incorporated by furnishing false information, which of the following orders can the Tribunal NOT pass under section 7(7)?

readLink.label: Read: The incorporation process — s. 7 →

options.text: An order regulating the management of the company, including changes in its memorandum and articles
options.explanation: Expressly available under s. 7(7)(a), in the public interest or in the interest of the company, its members and creditors.

options.text: An order that the liability of the members shall be unlimited
options.explanation: Expressly available under s. 7(7)(b).

options.text: An order declaring the certificate of incorporation void from the date of its issue, so that the company is deemed never to have existed
options.explanation: Section 7(7) has no such power. The Tribunal may remove the name or wind the company up PROSPECTIVELY, and is expressly directed to take into account the transactions the company has already entered into. Nothing is undone retrospectively.

options.text: An order for the winding up of the company
options.explanation: Expressly available under s. 7(7)(d), after a reasonable opportunity of being heard.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 7(5)–(6) · Who faces s. 447
questions.stem: A company is found to have been got incorporated by suppressing material facts. Under section 7(6), action under section 447 lies against:

readLink.label: Read: The incorporation process — s. 7 →

options.text: The company alone
options.explanation: Section 7(6) reaches the individuals behind the incorporation, not the company as the sole target.

options.text: The Registrar who registered the documents
options.explanation: The Registrar acts on the documents filed; s. 7 imposes no liability on him for having been deceived.

options.text: The subscribers only, and not the first directors
options.explanation: This is under-inclusive: first directors and the persons who made the s. 7(1)(b) declaration are named as well.

options.text: The promoters, the persons named as first directors and the persons making the declaration under section 7(1)(b)
options.explanation: That is the list in s. 7(6); separately, s. 7(5) catches any person who furnished false information or suppressed a material fact.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 4(1)(b) · Registered office clause
questions.stem: In relation to the registered office, the memorandum of association under section 4(1)(b) must state:

readLink.label: Read: The memorandum of association — s. 4 →

options.text: The full postal address of the registered office
options.explanation: The address is notified to the Registrar under s. 12; putting it in the memorandum would make every change of premises an alteration of the memorandum.

options.text: The State in which the registered office of the company is to be situated
options.explanation: Only the State. That is why a shift within the State is not an alteration of the memorandum, while a shift to another State is.

options.text: The city, town or village in which the registered office is to be situated
options.explanation: Local limits matter for the RESOLUTION needed under s. 12(5), but the memorandum names only the State.

options.text: The jurisdiction of the Registrar with whom the company is registered
options.explanation: The Registrar's jurisdiction decides where documents are filed and whether Regional Director confirmation is needed; it is not a memorandum clause.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 4(1)(e) · Subscription clause
questions.stem: In the case of a company having share capital, the memorandum must state the number of shares each subscriber to the memorandum agrees to subscribe, which shall not be less than:

readLink.label: Read: The memorandum of association — s. 4 →

options.text: One share
options.explanation: Each subscriber must take at least one share, and the memorandum records the number taken against his name.

options.text: Shares of the aggregate face value of ₹1,00,000
options.explanation: This revives the old minimum paid-up capital idea, which went with the omission of s. 11 in 2015. No rupee floor exists.

options.text: Ten shares
options.explanation: No such number appears in s. 4; the floor is one share per subscriber.

options.text: Five per cent of the authorised capital
options.explanation: A percentage of authorised capital is not a subscription requirement; the 5% figure belongs to application money under s. 39(2).

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 4(3) · Names suggesting government connection
questions.stem: A proposed name contains a word likely to give the impression that the company is connected with a State Government. Under section 4(3), such a name:

readLink.label: Read: The memorandum of association — s. 4 →

options.text: Is absolutely prohibited and can never be registered
options.explanation: It is not absolute — s. 4(3) permits registration where the previous approval of the Central Government has been obtained.

options.text: May be registered if the Registrar is satisfied that no member of the public will actually be misled
options.explanation: The Registrar's satisfaction is not the test; the section requires the Central Government's previous approval.

options.text: May be registered only with the previous approval of the Central Government
options.explanation: Section 4(3) bars such names unless the previous approval of the Central Government has been obtained; the same applies to prescribed words and expressions.

options.text: May be registered if a special resolution approving the name is passed by the subscribers
options.explanation: A resolution of the company cannot substitute for a governmental approval, and at the reservation stage there is no company to resolve.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 4(5)(i) · Name reservation, new company
questions.stem: A name is applied for on 8 September 2026 for a company proposed to be incorporated, and the Registrar approves the reservation on 14 September 2026. Ignoring any extension, the reservation is valid up to:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 4(5)(i) — 20 days from the date of approval

readLink.label: Read: The memorandum of association — s. 4 →

options.text: 28 September 2026
options.explanation: This counts the 20 days from the date of APPLICATION (8 September). Since the amendment, the period runs from the date of approval.

options.text: 4 October 2026
options.explanation: Twenty days from 14 September 2026, the date of approval — the period prescribed by s. 4(5)(i) for a proposed new company.

options.text: 13 November 2026
options.explanation: Sixty days from approval is the period for an EXISTING company applying to change its name, not for a proposed new company.

options.text: 14 October 2026
options.explanation: This reads the period as one calendar month. The section says twenty days.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 4(5)(i) proviso · Name reservation, existing company
questions.stem: Girnar Ceramics Limited, an existing company, applies to change its name and the Registrar approves the reservation on 20 January 2027. Ignoring any extension, the reserved name is available up to:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, proviso to s. 4(5)(i) — 60 days from the date of approval

readLink.label: Read: The memorandum of association — s. 4 →

options.text: 9 February 2027
options.explanation: Twenty days is the period for a proposed NEW company. An existing company changing its name gets sixty days.

options.text: 20 March 2027
options.explanation: This treats the period as two calendar months. The section prescribes sixty days, and 2027 is not a leap year, so the count lands a day later.

options.text: 21 March 2027
options.explanation: Sixty days from 20 January 2027 — 11 days of January, 28 of February and 21 of March.

options.text: 20 July 2027
options.explanation: Six months is not a period known to s. 4(5); it confuses the reservation window with the s. 3A grace period.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 4(5)(ii) · Name obtained by wrong information
questions.stem: A company has already been incorporated when it emerges that the name was reserved on the basis of wrong information. Under section 4(5)(ii), the Registrar, after giving the company an opportunity of being heard, may:

readLink.label: Read: The memorandum of association — s. 4 →

options.text: Direct the company to change its name within three months after passing an ordinary resolution, or take action for striking off, or make a petition for winding up
options.explanation: These are the three courses open under s. 4(5)(ii)(b) once the company is on the register.

options.text: Cancel the reserved name and impose a penalty of up to ₹1,00,000 on the applicant
options.explanation: That is the consequence where the company has NOT yet been incorporated, under s. 4(5)(ii)(a). Once incorporated there is a name in use, so the section switches to change, strike-off or winding up.

options.text: Direct a change of name within three months by a special resolution
options.explanation: The resolution required is an ORDINARY one — the company is obeying a direction, not exercising a free choice of name under s. 13(2).

options.text: Refer the matter to the Tribunal, which alone may order a change of name
options.explanation: No Tribunal reference is involved here. The NCLT enters only under s. 7(7), where the incorporation itself was obtained by fraud.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · ss. 4(6) and 5(6) · Schedule I Tables
questions.stem: Under the Companies Act 2013, the model forms of memorandum and of articles in Schedule I are respectively contained in:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, ss. 4(6) and 5(6), Schedule I

readLink.label: Read: The memorandum of association — s. 4 →

options.text: Tables A to E for articles and Tables F to J for memorandum
options.explanation: The two sets are the right ones but swapped. Memorandum comes first in the Act and first in the alphabet.

options.text: Tables A to E for memorandum and Tables F to J for articles
options.explanation: Section 4(6) points to Tables A to E for the memorandum and s. 5(6) to Tables F to J for the articles.

options.text: Table A for memorandum and Table F for articles, for every kind of company
options.explanation: Table A and Table F apply only to companies limited by shares; guarantee and unlimited companies have their own Tables.

options.text: Tables A to F for memorandum and Tables G to J for articles
options.explanation: Table F belongs to the articles set — it is the model articles for a company limited by shares.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 5(3)–(4) · Entrenchment
questions.stem: A private company wishes to insert provisions for entrenchment in its articles after incorporation. Section 5(4) requires:

readLink.label: Read: The articles of association — ss. 5 and 6 →

options.text: An ordinary resolution of the members
options.explanation: An ordinary resolution is nowhere near enough; entrenchment restricts the members' own future power to alter the articles.

options.text: A special resolution
options.explanation: A special resolution is what a PUBLIC company needs. For a private company s. 5(4) demands agreement of ALL the members.

options.text: The prior approval of the Tribunal
options.explanation: No Tribunal approval is involved. The only external step is notice of the entrenchment provisions to the Registrar under s. 5(5).

options.text: An amendment of the articles agreed to by all the members of the company
options.explanation: For a private company, entrenchment introduced after formation needs the agreement of all the members; a public company needs a special resolution.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 6 · Act overrides memorandum and articles
questions.stem: An article of a company confers on a shareholder a right that the Companies Act 2013 expressly denies. The consequence under section 6 is that:

readLink.label: Read: The articles of association — ss. 5 and 6 →

options.text: The article prevails, because the members are free to regulate their own affairs
options.explanation: Section 6 says the opposite: the Act has effect notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the articles.

options.text: The article prevails if it was registered before the commencement of the Act
options.explanation: Section 6 applies whether the document was registered or the resolution passed before or after the commencement of the Act.

options.text: The article is void to the extent to which it is repugnant to the Act
options.explanation: The Act overrides the memorandum, articles, agreements and resolutions, and the offending provision is void to the extent of the repugnancy — not the whole document.

options.text: The whole of the articles becomes void and the model articles apply instead
options.explanation: Section 6 strikes down only the repugnant provision; the rest of the articles survive.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 8 · Conditions for a licence
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a condition for the grant of a licence under section 8?

readLink.label: Read: Section 8 companies →

options.text: The company must be prohibited from paying any dividend to its members
options.explanation: Section 8(1)(c) requires exactly this prohibition.

options.text: The company must intend to apply its profits and other income only in promoting its objects
options.explanation: Section 8(1)(b) requires exactly this.

options.text: The objects must include the promotion of commerce, art, science, sports, education, research, social welfare, religion, charity, protection of the environment or any such other object
options.explanation: This is the objects list in s. 8(1)(a).

options.text: The company must be registered as a company limited by guarantee and must not have a share capital
options.explanation: Section 8 says nothing of the kind. A section 8 company may be limited by shares or by guarantee, public or private; what it may not do is pay a dividend.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 8(3)–(4) · Privileges and restrictions
questions.stem: Which statement about a section 8 company is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Section 8 companies →

options.text: It is exempt from the obligations of a limited company, because it works for charitable objects
options.explanation: Section 8(2) says it enjoys all the privileges AND is subject to all the obligations of a limited company.

options.text: A firm may be a member of it, and it may alter its memorandum or articles only with the previous approval of the Central Government
options.explanation: Both limbs are express: s. 8(3) allows a firm to be a member, and s. 8(4)(i) requires previous Central Government approval for any alteration.

options.text: It may alter its articles freely by special resolution like any other company
options.explanation: This ignores s. 8(4)(i), which superimposes previous Central Government approval on the ordinary s. 14 route.

options.text: A firm cannot be a member of it, since a firm is not a person
options.explanation: Section 8(3) makes a deliberate exception for section 8 companies — a firm may be a member.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 8(6) and 8(10) · Revocation and amalgamation
questions.stem: Regarding a section 8 company, which statement is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Section 8 companies →

options.text: The licence may be revoked where the company's affairs are conducted fraudulently or prejudicially to the public interest, after notice and an opportunity of being heard, and the company may amalgamate only with another section 8 company having similar objects
options.explanation: Section 8(6) sets out the revocation grounds and the hearing requirement; s. 8(10) confines amalgamation to another section 8 company with similar objects.

options.text: The licence may be revoked by the Registrar at any time without notice
options.explanation: Two errors: revocation is by the Central Government by order, and only after notice and an opportunity of being heard.

options.text: On revocation of the licence the company stands automatically dissolved
options.explanation: On revocation the Registrar puts 'Limited' or 'Private Limited' against the name; winding up requires a separate direction under s. 8(7).

options.text: A section 8 company may amalgamate with any company whose objects are commercially compatible
options.explanation: Section 8(10) is stricter — the other company must itself be a section 8 company AND have similar objects.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 9 · Effect of registration
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a consequence of registration under section 9 as it now stands?

readLink.label: Read: Effect of registration — ss. 9, 10 and 10A →

options.text: The subscribers and all persons who from time to time become members are a body corporate by the name contained in the memorandum
options.explanation: This is the opening limb of s. 9.

options.text: The company has perpetual succession and power to acquire, hold and dispose of property, to contract, and to sue and be sued
options.explanation: All expressly conferred by s. 9.

options.text: The company must have a common seal from the date of incorporation
options.explanation: The reference to a common seal was omitted from s. 9 by amendment — a seal is now OPTIONAL, which is why s. 22(2) provides for companies that have none.

options.text: The company becomes a body corporate from the date of incorporation mentioned in the certificate
options.explanation: Section 9 fixes the date of incorporation stated in the certificate as the moment corporate existence begins.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 10 · Binding effect of MOA and AOA
questions.stem: The articles of a company name a solicitor, who is also a member, as the company's solicitor for life. The company dismisses him and he sues on the article. Under section 10:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 10(1) — members bound qua members

readLink.label: Read: Effect of registration — ss. 9, 10 and 10A →

options.text: He succeeds, because the articles bind the company to each member as if signed by it
options.explanation: They do bind the company to members, but only in the member's capacity AS a member. His claim is as a solicitor.

options.text: He succeeds, because he is a member and the article is registered
options.explanation: Registration gives the article constructive notice, not enforceability in an outsider capacity.

options.text: He succeeds only if the article was entrenched
options.explanation: Entrenchment governs how an article may be ALTERED; it does not convert an outsider right into a contract.

options.text: He fails, because the articles bind the company to a member only in his capacity as a member, and his claim is in the capacity of a solicitor
options.explanation: Section 10 creates a contract between the company and the members qua members. A right claimed in an outsider capacity is unenforceable, even by someone who happens also to be a member.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 10A · The 180-day declaration
questions.stem: Suryodaya Infotech Private Limited, a company having share capital, is incorporated on 20 April 2026. The last date for filing the declaration for commencement of business under section 10A(1)(a) is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 10A(1)(a) — 180 days from the date of incorporation

readLink.label: Read: Effect of registration — ss. 9, 10 and 10A →

options.text: 19 July 2026
options.explanation: That is 90 days. Section 10A allows 180 days from the date of incorporation.

options.text: 20 October 2026
options.explanation: This reads 180 days as six calendar months. The section counts days, and 180 days from 20 April 2026 falls three days earlier.

options.text: 17 October 2026
options.explanation: 180 days from 20 April 2026 — 10 days of April, then May 31, June 30, July 31, August 31, September 30 and 17 of October.

options.text: 20 April 2027
options.explanation: One year is not a period known to s. 10A; the annual return timeline is being imported by mistake.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 10A(2)–(3) · Consequences of default
questions.stem: A company having share capital commences business without filing the declaration under section 10A. Which of the following is NOT a consequence?

readLink.label: Read: Effect of registration — ss. 9, 10 and 10A →

options.text: The transactions entered into by the company become void and unenforceable against it
options.explanation: Section 10A says nothing about the validity of the company's transactions. It imposes penalties and exposes the company to strike-off; contracts already made stand.

options.text: The company is liable to a penalty of ₹50,000
options.explanation: Expressly provided by s. 10A(2).

options.text: Every officer in default is liable to ₹1,000 for each day of continuing default, subject to a maximum of ₹1,00,000
options.explanation: Expressly provided by s. 10A(2).

options.text: Where no declaration is filed within 180 days and the Registrar has reasonable cause to believe the company is not carrying on business, he may initiate removal of its name from the register
options.explanation: Expressly provided by s. 10A(3), without prejudice to the penalties.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 11 omitted · Commencement of business
questions.stem: Which statement about the requirement to file a declaration before commencing business is correct for the law as on 28 February 2026?
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013 — s. 11 omitted; s. 10A inserted

readLink.label: Read: Effect of registration — ss. 9, 10 and 10A →

options.text: Section 11 stands omitted, and the requirement now lives in section 10A for companies incorporated after the 2018 amendment and having a share capital
options.explanation: Section 11 was omitted in 2015; s. 10A was inserted in 2018-19 with a narrower trigger — incorporation after that amendment, and a share capital.

options.text: Both section 11 and section 10A are in force, and a company must comply with each
options.explanation: Section 11 is not in force at all. Citing it in an answer is a straightforward mark loss.

options.text: Section 10A applies to every company, whether or not it has a share capital
options.explanation: Section 10A applies only to a company 'having a share capital'; a guarantee company without share capital is outside it.

options.text: Section 10A also prescribes a minimum paid-up capital of ₹1,00,000 for a private company
options.explanation: The minimum paid-up capital requirement went with the omission of s. 11 in 2015 and has not returned.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 12(2) · Verification of registered office
questions.stem: Anantha Foods Private Limited is incorporated on 3 August 2026. The last date by which it must furnish verification of its registered office to the Registrar under section 12(2) is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 12(2) — 30 days of incorporation

readLink.label: Read: Registered office — s. 12 →

options.text: 18 August 2026
options.explanation: Fifteen days was the position BEFORE the amendment that substituted thirty days in s. 12(1) and (2). Older material still says fifteen.

options.text: 1 September 2026
options.explanation: An off-by-one count. Twenty-eight days of August take the count to 31 August; two days of September complete the thirty.

options.text: 30 January 2027
options.explanation: 180 days is the s. 10A clock for the commencement declaration, not the s. 12(2) verification clock.

options.text: 2 September 2026
options.explanation: Thirty days from 3 August 2026. The same thirty-day period governs having a registered office at all under s. 12(1).

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 12(5) · Who approves a shift
questions.stem: A company wishes to shift its registered office from the jurisdiction of one Registrar to that of another Registrar within the same State. The approval required is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, proviso to s. 12(5) and s. 12(6)

readLink.label: Read: Registered office — s. 12 →

options.text: A special resolution of the members, confirmed by the Regional Director
options.explanation: The proviso to s. 12(5) requires confirmation by the Regional Director on top of the special resolution, and s. 12(6) then sets the 30 / 60 / 30-day clocks.

options.text: A Board resolution alone, since the State does not change
options.explanation: A Board resolution suffices only within the same city, town or village. Crossing Registrars needs a special resolution and RD confirmation.

options.text: A special resolution and the approval of the Central Government
options.explanation: Central Government approval belongs to a shift from one STATE to another under s. 13(4). Within a State the approver is the Regional Director.

options.text: A special resolution and confirmation by the Tribunal
options.explanation: The NCLT has no role in a registered-office shift; its incorporation-related jurisdiction is s. 7(7).

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 13(2)–(3) · Change of name
questions.stem: A company passes a special resolution to change its name and obtains the approval of the Central Government. The change of name is complete and effective:

readLink.label: Read: Alteration of the memorandum — s. 13 →

options.text: On the date the special resolution is passed
options.explanation: The resolution is only the first step; s. 13(2) then requires Central Government approval and s. 13(3) a fresh certificate.

options.text: On the date the Central Government approves the change
options.explanation: Approval clears the way but does not complete the change; s. 13(3) ties effectiveness to the issue of the fresh certificate.

options.text: On the date the special resolution is filed with the Registrar
options.explanation: Filing is a compliance step under s. 13(6), not the moment of effect.

options.text: Only on the issue by the Registrar of a fresh certificate of incorporation with the new name
options.explanation: Section 13(3) says the change is complete and effective ONLY on the issue of that certificate. Note also the proviso to s. 13(2): no approval is needed where the only change is adding or deleting 'Private' on a conversion of class.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 14 · Public to private conversion
questions.stem: An alteration of articles having the effect of converting a public company into a private company is not valid unless approved by:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, second proviso to s. 14(1)

readLink.label: Read: Alteration of articles, noting and conversion →

options.text: An order of the Central Government, the power being exercised by the Regional Director
options.explanation: The second proviso to s. 14(1) named the Tribunal when first enacted; an amendment Act substituted the Central Government, whose power is delegated to the Regional Director.

options.text: An order of the Tribunal
options.explanation: This is the pre-amendment position that older banks still carry. The Tribunal now retains only applications that were already pending before it.

options.text: The Registrar of Companies
options.explanation: The Registrar registers the altered articles under s. 14(2); he does not approve the conversion.

options.text: No approval — a special resolution suffices for any alteration of articles
options.explanation: A special resolution is necessary but not sufficient here; the conversion also needs the Central Government's order.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 16 · Rectification of name
questions.stem: The Central Government directs a company under section 16(1) to change a name that too nearly resembles that of an existing company. Which statement is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Rectification of name — s. 16 →

options.text: The company must change its name within six months of the direction, by special resolution
options.explanation: Both figures are the pre-amendment ones. The period is now three months, and the resolution is an ordinary one.

options.text: The company must change its name within three months of the direction, by special resolution
options.explanation: The period is right but the resolution is wrong — s. 16(1) requires only an ORDINARY resolution, because the company is complying with a direction.

options.text: If the company defaults, it is punishable with a fine, but its name cannot be changed without its consent
options.explanation: This is the old s. 16(3). As substituted, the Central Government itself ALLOTS a new name and the Registrar issues a fresh certificate of incorporation.

options.text: The company must change its name within three months of the direction, after passing an ordinary resolution, and give notice of the change to the Registrar within fifteen days
options.explanation: Three months by ordinary resolution under s. 16(1), and notice with the Central Government's order within fifteen days of the change under s. 16(2).

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Doctrine of constructive notice
questions.stem: The doctrine of constructive notice means that:
questions.sourceRef: ICAI SM P2 Ch 2 — doctrine of constructive notice

readLink.label: Read: The three doctrines →

options.text: The company is deemed to have notice of the affairs of every person who deals with it
options.explanation: The doctrine runs the other way — it is the outsider who is fixed with notice of the company's public documents.

options.text: Every person dealing with the company is deemed to have notice of the contents of its registered memorandum and articles, whether or not he has read them
options.explanation: The memorandum and articles are public documents open to inspection, so notice of their contents — and of their proper meaning — is imputed to outsiders. The doctrine protects the company.

options.text: An outsider is entitled to assume that the internal proceedings of the company have been regularly carried out
options.explanation: That is the doctrine of INDOOR MANAGEMENT, the counterweight to constructive notice, and it protects the outsider rather than the company.

options.text: A member is deemed to have notice of every resolution passed by the Board
options.explanation: Board resolutions are not public documents; constructive notice attaches to documents registered with the Registrar and open to inspection.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Doctrine of ultra vires
questions.stem: A company enters into a transaction wholly outside its objects clause. All the shareholders later approve it unanimously at a general meeting. The transaction is:
questions.sourceRef: ICAI SM P2 Ch 2 — doctrine of ultra vires; Ashbury Railway Carriage & Iron Co Ltd v Riche

readLink.label: Read: The three doctrines →

options.text: Valid, because the shareholders are the ultimate owners and their unanimous assent cures any defect
options.explanation: Shareholders cannot confer on the company a capacity the memorandum never gave it; that is the whole holding in Ashbury v Riche.

options.text: Voidable at the option of the company
options.explanation: It is void, not voidable. A voidable transaction presupposes capacity to make it in the first place.

options.text: Void, and incapable of ratification even by the unanimous vote of all the shareholders
options.explanation: An act ultra vires the COMPANY is void ab initio and unratifiable. Only an act ultra vires the DIRECTORS, or irregular under the articles, can be ratified by the members.

options.text: Valid, provided the company alters its objects clause afterwards under section 13
options.explanation: A later alteration of objects operates prospectively once registered; it cannot validate a transaction that was void when made.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Case: incorporation obtained by false information
questions.case: Vaanya Renewables Limited was incorporated on 15 April 2026. To secure registration, two of its subscribers filed identity documents that they knew to be forged, and the practising company secretary engaged in the formation signed the declaration under section 7(1)(b) without verifying anything. The name 'Vaanya Renewables' had itself been reserved on the strength of a statement about the applicants' existing business that was untrue. On a complaint by a creditor, the Registrar begins proceedings; separately, an application is made to the Tribunal in respect of the incorporation. On 6 July 2026 the Registrar, after hearing the company, directs it to change its name under section 4(5)(ii)(b).

readLink.label: Read: The incorporation process — s. 7 →

questions.stem: Action under section 447 in respect of the false identity documents lies against:

options.text: The subscribers who furnished the false documents, and — because the company was got incorporated by those means — also the promoters, the persons named as first directors and the company secretary who made the section 7(1)(b) declaration
options.explanation: Section 7(5) catches the person who furnishes false information; s. 7(6) extends liability to promoters, first directors and the declarants once the company has been got incorporated by such means.

options.text: The subscribers alone, since only they furnished false documents
options.explanation: This ignores s. 7(6), which is triggered by the fact that the company was got incorporated by fraudulent means and names three further categories.

options.text: The company alone, as a body corporate answerable for the acts of its subscribers
options.explanation: Section 7(5) and 7(6) fasten on individuals. The company's own fate is dealt with by the Tribunal under s. 7(7).

options.text: No one, because the certificate of incorporation has already been issued
options.explanation: Issue of the certificate is precisely the situation ss. 7(6) and 7(7) address; it confers no immunity.

questions.stem: On the application before it, the Tribunal may pass any of the following orders EXCEPT:

options.text: An order regulating the management of the company, including changes in its memorandum and articles
options.explanation: Available under s. 7(7)(a).

options.text: A direction that the liability of the members shall be unlimited
options.explanation: Available under s. 7(7)(b).

options.text: An order treating every contract entered into by the company since 15 April 2026 as void ab initio
options.explanation: Section 7(7) contains no such power. Its proviso in fact directs the Tribunal to TAKE INTO ACCOUNT the transactions the company has entered into, including obligations contracted and liabilities paid, before removing the name or winding up.

options.text: An order for the removal of the name of the company from the register of companies
options.explanation: Available under s. 7(7)(c), after a reasonable opportunity of being heard.

questions.stem: Following the Registrar's direction of 6 July 2026 under section 4(5)(ii)(b), the company must change its name by:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 4(5)(ii)(b)(i) — three months from the direction

options.text: 21 July 2026
options.explanation: Fifteen days is the s. 16(2) period for giving NOTICE of a change already made, not the period for making the change.

options.text: 6 October 2026
options.explanation: Three calendar months from 6 July 2026, the date of the direction, and the change is made after passing an ordinary resolution.

options.text: 6 January 2027
options.explanation: Six months is the pre-amendment figure in the parallel s. 16 provision; s. 4(5)(ii) allows three months.

options.text: 6 September 2026
options.explanation: Two months is not a period known to the section; the count is three months from the direction.

questions.stem: The resolution the company must pass to effect the change of name directed by the Registrar is:

options.text: A Board resolution only
options.explanation: The change of a company's name is a members' matter; the Board alone cannot do it.

options.text: A special resolution, together with the approval of the Central Government
options.explanation: That is the route for a name change the company itself initiates under s. 13(2). Here the company is obeying a direction, so the lighter route applies.

options.text: An ordinary resolution
options.explanation: Section 4(5)(ii)(b)(i) requires the change to be made 'after adopting an ordinary resolution' — the same lighter requirement as in s. 16(1).

options.text: A unanimous resolution of all the members
options.explanation: Unanimity is required only where the articles are entrenched under s. 5(4) in a private company; it has no place here.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Case: indoor management, constructive notice and ultra vires
questions.case: The articles of Hemadri Steels Limited authorise the Board to borrow up to ₹50 lakh, and beyond that only after an ordinary resolution of the members. Its memorandum limits its objects to the manufacture and sale of steel products. In June 2026 the Board borrows ₹1.2 crore from Trishul Finance Ltd against a bond signed by two directors; no members' resolution was in fact passed, though the bond recites that one was. Trishul Finance is also handed, as additional comfort, a certificate for 20,000 shares of Hemadri Steels on which the company secretary's signature has been forged by a clerk. Later the same year, the Board applies ₹35 lakh of the borrowed money to acquire a hotel property, an activity wholly outside the objects clause; ₹15 lakh of the borrowing had, however, been used to pay off a genuine trade creditor of the company.

readLink.label: Read: The three doctrines →

questions.stem: As to the borrowing of ₹1.2 crore, the position of Trishul Finance Ltd is that:
questions.sourceRef: ICAI SM P2 Ch 2 — Royal British Bank v Turquand

options.text: It cannot enforce the bond, because it is deemed by constructive notice to know that a members' resolution was required
options.explanation: Constructive notice fixes it with knowledge of the REQUIREMENT, but whether the resolution was actually passed is an internal matter it cannot check.

options.text: It cannot enforce the bond, because a borrowing beyond the limit in the articles is ultra vires the company
options.explanation: Exceeding a borrowing limit in the ARTICLES is ultra vires the directors, not the company; the objects clause is what fixes corporate capacity.

options.text: It can enforce the bond only up to ₹50 lakh, the limit stated in the articles
options.explanation: The rule does not scale the contract down to the Board's unaided authority; the whole bond binds the company unless an exception applies.

options.text: It can enforce the bond, being entitled to assume that the required members' resolution was duly passed
options.explanation: This is Turquand's rule: an outsider is bound by what the constitution says but may presume that its internal procedure was complied with.

questions.stem: As to the share certificate carrying the forged signature, Trishul Finance Ltd:
questions.sourceRef: ICAI SM P2 Ch 2 — forgery as an exception to indoor management

options.text: Acquires no title to the shares, because a forgery is a nullity and there is no act of the company for the rule of indoor management to regularise
options.explanation: Forgery is the clearest exception: the doctrine presumes an act of the company that is merely irregular internally, and a forged document is no act at all.

options.text: Acquires good title, because it acted in good faith and without notice of the forgery
options.explanation: Good faith does not help. The exception applies however innocent the holder is.

options.text: Acquires good title, because the certificate was issued by an officer of the company
options.explanation: The signature was forged by a clerk; there was no genuine execution by an authorised officer at all.

options.text: Acquires title only if the company subsequently ratifies the issue of the certificate
options.explanation: A nullity cannot be ratified into existence; the company may choose to issue fresh shares, but that is a new act, not ratification.

questions.stem: As to the ₹35 lakh applied to acquire the hotel property:
questions.sourceRef: ICAI SM P2 Ch 2 — consequences of an ultra vires act

options.text: The acquisition is valid, since the money used was validly borrowed
options.explanation: The source of the money is irrelevant to capacity; an application outside the objects is outside the company's powers.

options.text: The acquisition is voidable at the instance of the members in general meeting
options.explanation: It is void, not voidable, and members cannot validate it however they vote.

options.text: The acquisition is valid if ratified by a special resolution altering the objects clause
options.explanation: An alteration of objects under s. 13 operates prospectively from registration; it cannot retrospectively validate a void act.

options.text: The acquisition is ultra vires the company and void; the directors are personally liable to restore the amount, and any member may seek an injunction
options.explanation: These are the standard consequences of an act beyond the objects clause. The property acquired nevertheless remains the company's property.

questions.stem: Assume instead that the ENTIRE borrowing had been ultra vires the company. As to the ₹15 lakh used to pay off a genuine trade creditor, the lender's best position would be:
questions.sourceRef: ICAI SM P2 Ch 2 — remedies on an ultra vires borrowing

options.text: To sue the company on the loan agreement, which remains enforceable to that extent
options.explanation: An ultra vires borrowing is void; no part of it can be sued on as a contract.

options.text: To claim subrogation to the rights of the trade creditor whose lawful debt was discharged with its money
options.explanation: Equity substitutes the lender for the creditor who was paid off, to the extent of the intra vires debt discharged; separately, it may trace its money or the property bought with it while identifiable.

options.text: To petition the Tribunal to declare the company's incorporation void
options.explanation: That confuses an ultra vires borrowing with a fraudulently obtained incorporation under s. 7(7) — and even there, no retrospective avoidance is available.

options.text: To recover from the members personally, since the borrowing was for the company's benefit
options.explanation: Members' liability is limited; it is the DIRECTORS who may be personally liable, for breach of warranty of authority and to restore the company's funds.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Case: registered-office shift and change of name timelines
questions.case: Panchganga Chemicals Limited has its registered office at Nashik, within the jurisdiction of one Registrar in Maharashtra, and resolves by special resolution to shift it to Aurangabad, within the jurisdiction of a different Registrar in the same State. It applies to the Regional Director, who communicates his confirmation on 4 May 2026. Quite separately, the Central Government had earlier directed the company under section 16(1) to change its name because it too nearly resembled that of an existing company; the company duly changes its name on 18 August 2026 after passing the required resolution.

readLink.label: Read: Registered office — s. 12 →

questions.stem: The last date by which the company must file the Regional Director's confirmation with the Registrar is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 12(6) — 60 days from the date of confirmation

options.text: 3 June 2026
options.explanation: Thirty days is the period within which the Regional Director must COMMUNICATE the confirmation, not the period for the company to file it.

options.text: 3 July 2026
options.explanation: Sixty days from 4 May 2026 — 27 days of May, 30 of June and 3 of July. The Registrar then registers and certifies within thirty days of this filing.

options.text: 4 July 2026
options.explanation: This treats the period as two calendar months rather than sixty days, giving one day too many.

options.text: 2 August 2026
options.explanation: Ninety days is not a period known to s. 12(6); the three periods there are 30, 60 and 30 days.

questions.stem: Having changed its name on 18 August 2026 pursuant to the section 16(1) direction, the company must give notice of the change to the Registrar by:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 16(2) — 15 days from the date of the change

options.text: 17 September 2026
options.explanation: Thirty days is the s. 12(4) period for notice of a change of the SITUATION of the registered office, not the s. 16(2) period.

options.text: 1 September 2026
options.explanation: An off-by-one count: thirteen days of August take the count to 31 August, and two days of September complete the fifteen.

options.text: 18 November 2026
options.explanation: Three months is the period allowed to MAKE the change under s. 16(1); notice of the change already made is due much sooner.

options.text: 2 September 2026
options.explanation: Fifteen days from 18 August 2026, and the notice must be accompanied by the Central Government's order.

questions.stem: Which statement about the two matters is correct?

options.text: The shift from Nashik to Aurangabad is not an alteration of the memorandum, since the memorandum states only the State; and the change of name directed under section 16 needs only an ordinary resolution
options.explanation: Both limbs are right. The memorandum names the State alone, so an intra-State shift is outside s. 13; and a change of name made in obedience to a s. 16(1) direction is effected by ordinary resolution.

options.text: Both matters require a special resolution and the approval of the Central Government
options.explanation: Central Government approval belongs to a State-to-State shift (s. 13(4)) and to a company-initiated change of name (s. 13(2)); neither is the position here.

options.text: The shift requires confirmation by the Tribunal, and the change of name a special resolution
options.explanation: The confirming authority for an intra-State inter-Registrar shift is the Regional Director, and the s. 16 change needs only an ordinary resolution.

options.text: The shift takes effect from the date of the special resolution, and the change of name from the date of the direction
options.explanation: The shift takes effect from the date of the Registrar's certificate under s. 12(7); a change of name is complete only on a fresh certificate of incorporation.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · ss. 3 and 3A · Formation and reduction of membership
questions.stem: State the minimum number of persons required to form each class of company under section 3 of the Companies Act 2013, and explain the consequences under section 3A where the number of members of a company falls below that minimum and the company continues to carry on business. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 3(1): seven or more persons for a public company; two or more for a private company; one person for a One Person Company, which is formed as a private company; formation is by subscribing names to a memorandum and complying with the registration requirements
Section 3(2): the company so formed may be limited by shares, limited by guarantee, or unlimited — a classification by liability, independent of the number of subscribers
Section 3A trigger: members reduced below seven (public) or below two (private) AND the company carries on business for more than six months while so reduced

Consequence: every person who is a member during the time the company so carries on business after those six months, and who is cognisant of the fact, is severally liable for the payment of the whole of the debts of the company contracted during that time, and may be severally sued therefor

Points to note: the company is not dissolved and its separate personality continues; a member who is not cognisant of the reduction escapes; debts contracted before the six months expire are unaffected; liability is several, not joint
skeleton.citation: ICAI SM P2 Ch 2 — analysis of s. 3A

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 2(69) · Promoters and pre-incorporation contracts
questions.stem: Define 'promoter' under section 2(69) of the Companies Act 2013. Explain the legal position of a promoter in relation to the company he promotes, and state the effect of a contract entered into by promoters before incorporation. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Definition: a person (a) named as a promoter in a prospectus or identified as such by the company in the annual return under s. 92; or (b) who has control over the affairs of the company, directly or indirectly, whether as shareholder, director or otherwise; or (c) in accordance with whose advice, directions or instructions the Board is accustomed to act
Proviso: a person acting merely in a professional capacity is not a promoter — e.g. the solicitor, chartered accountant or banker advising on the formation

Legal position: a promoter is neither an agent nor a trustee of the company, since the company is not in existence, but he stands in a fiduciary relation to it — he must not make a secret profit, must disclose any interest in transactions with the company to an independent Board or to the members, and must account
skeleton.citation: ICAI SM P2 Ch 2 — fiduciary position of promoters

skeleton.point: Remedies for breach: rescission of the contract; recovery of the secret profit while retaining the property; or damages for breach of fiduciary duty. A promoter has no legal right to preliminary expenses or remuneration unless the company chooses to pay

Pre-incorporation contracts: not binding on the company, which was not in existence; the company cannot ratify such a contract; the promoters remain personally liable; the company may become bound by entering into a fresh contract (novation) after incorporation
skeleton.citation: ICAI SM P2 Ch 2 — preliminary contracts

skeleton.point: Statutory exception: under ss. 15(h) and 19(e) of the Specific Relief Act 1963 the contract may be specifically enforced by or against the company where it is warranted by the terms of the incorporation and the company has accepted it and communicated the acceptance to the other party

questions.topic: Ch 2 · s. 7 · Incorporation and its consequences
questions.stem: List the documents and information to be filed with the Registrar for the incorporation of a company under section 7(1) of the Companies Act 2013, and state the consequences where a company has been got incorporated by furnishing false or incorrect information. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Filing is with the Registrar within whose jurisdiction the registered office is proposed to be situated; the memorandum and articles, duly signed by all subscribers in the prescribed manner, head the list

Declaration by an advocate, chartered accountant, cost accountant or company secretary in practice engaged in the formation, and by a person named in the articles as a director, manager or secretary, that all requirements of the Act and rules as to registration are complied with

Declaration by each subscriber and each first director: no conviction for an offence in connection with the promotion, formation or management of any company; no finding of fraud, misfeasance or breach of duty to any company in the preceding five years; and that all documents filed contain correct and complete information

Address for correspondence till the registered office is established; particulars and proof of identity of every subscriber (with prescribed particulars where a subscriber is a body corporate); particulars of the first directors with DIN and proof of identity; and particulars of their interests in other firms or bodies corporate with their consent to act

On registration the Registrar issues the certificate of incorporation and allots a Corporate Identity Number; the company must maintain and preserve copies of all documents and information filed until its dissolution

False information: the person furnishing it is liable under s. 447 (s. 7(5)); where the company was got incorporated by such means, the promoters, the persons named as first directors and the persons making the s. 7(1)(b) declaration are liable under s. 447 (s. 7(6)); and the Tribunal may, after a hearing, regulate the management including changes to the memorandum and articles, direct that members' liability be unlimited, direct removal of the name, order winding up, or pass any other fit order, taking into account transactions already entered into (s. 7(7))

questions.topic: Ch 2 · ss. 4 and 5 · Memorandum, articles and entrenchment
questions.stem: State the clauses that the memorandum of association of a company must contain under section 4(1). Explain the restrictions on the choice of name under sections 4(2) and 4(3) and the periods for which a name may be reserved, and state what provisions for entrenchment are and how they may be introduced. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Clauses: name (with 'Limited' or 'Private Limited', section 8 companies excepted); the State in which the registered office is to be situated; the objects and matters considered necessary in furtherance thereof; the liability of members (limited by shares to the amount unpaid, or the guarantee amount); for a company with share capital, the authorised capital divided into shares of a fixed amount and the shares each subscriber takes, not less than one each; and for an OPC, the nominee

Section 4(2): the name must not be identical with or too nearly resemble the name of an existing company, must not constitute an offence under any law, and must not be undesirable in the opinion of the Central Government

Section 4(3): a name suggesting connection with, or the patronage of, the Central or a State Government, a local authority or a statutory body, or containing a prescribed word or expression, requires the previous approval of the Central Government

Reservation under s. 4(5): twenty days from the date of approval for a proposed new company, and sixty days from the date of approval where an existing company applies for a change of name; consequences of wrong information — cancellation and penalty up to ₹1,00,000 before incorporation, and after incorporation a direction to change the name within three months by ordinary resolution, striking off, or a winding-up petition

Entrenchment: provisions under which specified articles may be altered only on conditions or procedures more restrictive than a special resolution; they may be made on formation or by amendment agreed to by all the members of a private company or by special resolution in a public company; and notice of the provisions must be given to the Registrar in the prescribed form and manner

questions.topic: Ch 2 · ss. 12 and 13 · Registered office and alteration of the memorandum
questions.stem: Explain the requirements of section 12 as to the registered office of a company, and set out the approvals and procedure for shifting the registered office (a) within the same city, (b) from the jurisdiction of one Registrar to another within the same State and (c) from one State to another. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 12(1)–(2): a company must have a registered office capable of receiving and acknowledging all communications within thirty days of incorporation and at all times thereafter, and must furnish verification of that office to the Registrar within thirty days of incorporation

Section 12(3): painting or affixing the name and registered-office address outside every place of business in legible letters (and in the characters of the local language where needed); engraving the name on the seal, if any; printing the name, address, CIN, telephone, fax, e-mail and website on business letters, billheads, notices and official publications; printing the name on hundies, promissory notes and bills of exchange; the former name to be shown for two years after a change; and '(One Person Company)' below the name of an OPC
(a) Within the same city, town or village: a Board resolution suffices, and notice of the change of situation is given to the Registrar within thirty days of the change under s. 12(4)

(b) Beyond local limits, and from one Registrar's jurisdiction to another within the same State: a special resolution under s. 12(5), and in the latter case confirmation by the Regional Director; the Regional Director communicates confirmation within thirty days of receipt of the application, the company files it with the Registrar within sixty days of the date of confirmation, and the Registrar registers and certifies within thirty days of that filing, the certificate being conclusive evidence of compliance and the change taking effect from its date

(c) From one State to another: this is an alteration of the memorandum needing a special resolution under s. 13(1) and the approval of the Central Government under s. 13(4); the application is disposed of within sixty days, and before approving, the Central Government may satisfy itself as to the consent of creditors, debenture-holders and other persons concerned, or that sufficient provision or adequate security exists for the discharge of debts; a certified copy of the order is filed with the Registrar of each State and the Registrar of the new State issues a fresh certificate of incorporation

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Doctrines of constructive notice, indoor management and ultra vires
questions.stem: Explain the doctrines of constructive notice and indoor management, stating the exceptions to the latter. Explain also the doctrine of ultra vires and the consequences of an ultra vires transaction. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Constructive notice: the memorandum and articles are public documents registered with the Registrar and open to inspection, so every person dealing with the company is deemed to have notice of their contents and to have understood them properly; the doctrine protects the company against outsiders
skeleton.citation: ICAI SM P2 Ch 2 — doctrine of constructive notice

skeleton.point: Indoor management: as laid down in Royal British Bank v Turquand, an outsider dealing with the company is entitled to assume that the internal proceedings and procedures required by the constitution have been duly complied with, and is not bound to enquire into their regularity; the doctrine protects the outsider
skeleton.citation: ICAI SM P2 Ch 2 — Royal British Bank v Turquand

skeleton.point: Exceptions: actual knowledge of the irregularity; circumstances arousing suspicion, where the outsider fails to make enquiry; forgery, which is a nullity and not an irregularity; absence of any reliance on the articles by the person dealing with the company; and acts which are void in themselves, including acts ultra vires the company
skeleton.citation: ICAI SM P2 Ch 2 — exceptions to indoor management

skeleton.point: Ultra vires: the objects clause fixes the company's capacity, and an act beyond it is void and cannot be ratified even by the unanimous vote of all the shareholders (Ashbury Railway Carriage & Iron Co Ltd v Riche); what is fairly incidental to or consequential upon the stated objects is intra vires
skeleton.citation: ICAI SM P2 Ch 2 — Ashbury v Riche

skeleton.point: Consequences: any member may obtain an injunction to restrain the act; the directors are personally liable to restore the funds and compensate the company, and may be sued for breach of warranty of authority; on an ultra vires borrowing the lender cannot sue on the loan but may trace his money or the property acquired with it while identifiable, and may be subrogated to a lawful creditor whose intra vires debt was discharged; property acquired ultra vires nevertheless remains the property of the company
skeleton.citation: ICAI SM P2 Ch 2 — consequences of ultra vires acts
